title: Duterte in ICC jail, but families still afraid – Callamard
summary: 'How can it be that years after the killings, accountability here is still not possible?' asks Amnesty International secretary general Agnes Callamard

items: Former President Rodrigo Duterte is detained in The Hague, but families of victims from his anti-drug campaign still fear seeking justice in the Philippines.
Amnesty International's Agnès Callamard highlighted the ongoing lack of accountability for the killings, questioning why justice remains elusive despite Duterte's trial for crimes against humanity.
The launch of 'Walang Pahimakas,' an anthology of poems honoring the victims, emphasizes the importance of remembrance and the need for independent investigations into unlawful killings.

QUEZON CITY, Philippines – Former president Rodrigo Duterte is detained in The Hague, but the families of those killed in his war on drugs are still afraid to seek justice in the Philippines.
Nearly a decade after the killings began, their fear has not gone away.
“How can it be that Duterte is in prison in The Hague, and yet people are scared here now?” Amnesty International secretary general Agnès Callamard asked Friday, November 20.

Callamard, returning to the Philippines after a Duterte-era immigration ban was lifted, raised the question during the launch of Walang Pahimakas (No Farewell), an anthology of poems remembering those killed in the anti-drug campaign.

blocks.caption: REMEMBERING. Amnesty International officials and editors of Walang Pahimakas discuss poetry, remembrance, and accountability for drug war killings, on November 20, 2026. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

blocks.text: She had spent the previous 48 hours meeting victims’ families. Their message, she said, was that justice remained beyond their reach.
“How can it be that years after the killings, accountability here is still not possible?” she asked.
“That is an indictment not of President Duterte. It is an indictment of the current government.”
Her remarks came 10 days before the scheduled opening of Duterte’s trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on November 30.

The former president faces charges of crimes against humanity, including murder and attempted murder, over killings allegedly committed during his anti-drug campaign and earlier operations in Davao City. He has denied wrongdoing.

Callamard welcomed the coming proceedings but said the Marcos administration must also deliver accountability through independent investigations, witness protection, and prosecution of those responsible for unlawful killings.

At the book launch in Quezon City, National Artist for Literature Virgilio Almario, better known as Rio Alma, read his poem Pag Nahimlay ang Katwiran (Pagkatapos ni Francisco Goya), written on May 3, 2020.

blocks.caption: RIO ALMA. National Artist for Literature Virgilio Almario reads his poem Pag Nahimlay ang Katwiran, a warning against injustice and abuse of power, on November 20, 2026. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

blocks.text: “Pag nahimlay ang katwiran, lumalabas ang halimaw.” (When reason falls asleep, the monster emerges.)
Cordilleran poet Susie Bangles-Baldo, writing as Layad Ya Ikigai, read Magay Inges Na Ay Sakit, a poem in Kankanaey about a family whose hopes for their child’s future are shattered by loss.

blocks.caption: POETRY. Cordilleran poet Susie Bangles-Baldo reads her Kankanaey poem Magay Inges Na Ay Sakit, a story of sacrifice, hope, and loss, on November 20, 2026. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

blocks.text: Their works are among those featured in Walang Pahimakas, Amnesty International Philippines’ first published book, with contributions from more than 70 writers and artists.

First unveiled at the Manila International Book Fair in September, the anthology tells the stories of people whose deaths were often reduced to police reports, statistics, and the familiar claim that suspects had fought back.
Its editors, poets Ronald Atilano and Harold Fiesta, said the collection challenges the narratives that helped normalize the killings.
Atilano described the poems as testimony against forgetting, recalling how violence could be presented as necessary or even as service to the nation.
Fiesta said poetry could not bring back the dead, but it could keep their stories from disappearing.
“Those who were denied a proper goodbye should not also be denied remembrance,” he said.
During the launch, Amnesty presented a symbolic check for P69,300 to representatives of victims’ families, representing sales of Walang Pahimakas and Suong at the Manila International Book Fair.

blocks.caption: SUPPORT. Amnesty International presents ₱69,300 in proceeds from book sales at the Manila International Book Fair to support families of drug war victims, on November 20, 2026. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

blocks.text: Callamard last visited the Philippines in 2017, when she was serving as United Nations special rapporteur on extrajudicial executions.

Her criticism of Duterte’s anti-drug campaign and calls for an investigation into the killings drew the administration’s ire. In 2018, she was barred from entering the country and declared an undesirable alien.
The immigration restriction was lifted in September 2026.
“A ban may keep a person out, but it cannot suppress the truth,” she said.
Callamard’s return comes as Duterte faces proceedings before the ICC, which is investigating alleged crimes committed while the Philippines was still a party to the Rome Statute.

blocks.caption: Duterte in ICC jail, but families still afraid – Callamard

blocks.text: Police figures recorded more than 6,000 deaths during anti-drug operations under Duterte. Human rights organizations have estimated a much higher toll, including killings attributed to unidentified assailants.
Amnesty International Philippines section director Ritz Lee Santos III said accountability through Philippine courts remains limited.

Citing the organization’s assessment, Santos said only five cases involving nine police officers had resulted in convictions, despite thousands of deaths. (READ: [Pinoy Criminology] The hidden impact of Duterte’s drug war)
He questioned how families could pursue justice when filing complaints meant spending money on transportation, missing work, and risking their safety.
“A mother should be able to ask these questions without being passed from one office to another,” he said.

Amnesty International called on the government to investigate unlawful killings, protect witnesses, and replace punitive drug policies with voluntary treatment, healthcare, and evidence-based harm reduction programs.
Callamard, who plans to attend the opening of Duterte’s trial in The Hague, said international proceedings should not become an excuse for inaction in the Philippines.

She also warned that sanctions and political pressure against the ICC, particularly from the United States, threatened an institution on which victims of serious crimes depend when domestic justice systems fail them.

As the launch ended, the poems returned attention to the people at the center of the case: children who waited for parents who never came home, families still looking for answers, and survivors who remain afraid to speak.
Callamard promised them that Amnesty International would continue pressing for investigations and accountability.
“You are not alone, we stand by you and we will fight with you.” – Rappler.com
